tables.title: The Alphabet
tables.intro: Where a letter has two values, the first is with a dagesh and the second without (rafe). Following the Talmud (Shabbath 104a), the ordinary forms of נ פ צ are kĕfufa (bent) and their final forms pĕshuṭa (straight); ך follows the same pattern. Open מ is pĕthuḥa and closed ם is sĕthuma.
rows: the catch in your throat in “uh-oh”
“g” in go / Arabic غ (ghayn), a voiced gargle from the back of the throat
Arabic ح (ḥāʾ): the breath you use to fog up glasses
Arabic ط (ṭāʾ): a “t” with the tongue tensed and pulled back
“k” in kite / Arabic خ (khāʾ), like “ch” in German Bach
Arabic ع (ʿayn): a voiced tightening deep in the throat
Arabic ص (ṣād): a tensed “s”, tongue pulled back
Arabic ق (qāf): a “k” made further back in the throat
a tongue-tip r, tapped or trilled, as in Spanish pero / perro

tables.title: The Five Groups
tables.intro: Tradition sorts the letters by where in the mouth they are made: אחה״ע גיכ״ק דטלנ״ת זסשר״ץ בומ״ף (Ibn Ezra on Shemoth 3:15). It is the traditional classification, not modern phonetics, but it explains why ח and ע stay throat sounds and why ו belongs with the lips.
rows: g gh y k kh q
back of the tongue against the palate
d dh ṭ l n t th
the teeth, with a hissing or whistling sound
b v w m p f

notes.title: Special Cases
items: Divine Name. The Divine Name (י״י / יְיָ) always renders as “Adhonay”, whatever its vocalization in the source text.
Qamaṣ qaṭan is written o: כָּל is kol, חָכְמָה is ḥokhma.
Doubled letters. A dagesh that doubles a letter is written as a doubled letter: שַׁבָּת is shabbath.
Mappiq. A word-final ה with a mappiq is pronounced and written h: אַרְצָהּ is ʾarṣah. Otherwise final ה is silent.
Long i. A ḥireq without a yod is sometimes written ī, where the syllable division treats it as long: שָׁמַיִם is shamayīm, דָּוִד is dawīdh. Say it the same as i.
Silent shĕwa is not written: מַלְכּוּת is malkuth.

notes.title: About the Letter Names
items: The names follow the list Baghdadi teachers used when teaching children the alphabet, as recorded by Jacob Mansour (The Jewish Baghdadi Dialect, 1991). Where a name looks shorter than the school form (Be, Dal, Zan, 'An, Ṣad, Ta), that is the traditional form; the same shortened pattern is described for Yemenite tradition.

Modern equivalents: ʾAlef = Alef, Be = Bet, Gimal = Gimel, Dal = Dalet, Zan = Zayin, Ḥeth = Het, Ṭeth = Tet, Lamad = Lamed, Mim = Mem, Sĕmmakh = Samekh, 'An = Ayin, Ṣad = Tsadi, Rosh = Resh, Ta = Tav.

notes.title: Notes on Pronunciation
items: w and th/dh are kept. Iraqi tradition keeps the classical w for waw and the interdental sounds for rafe dal and rafe ta, which most other communities have lost.

Throat letters and emphatics. ḥ and ' are true throat sounds, and ṭ and ṣ are emphatic, as in Arabic. Ibn Ezra already remarks that ח and ע are “very heavy”, and that someone who did not grow up saying them cannot pronounce them as Arabic speakers do.
Qof. q is a deep stop at the back of the throat, distinct from k.

Rosh. r is made with the tip of the tongue, tapped or trilled, never the French- or Israeli-style r in the back of the throat. That keeps it with the other tongue-and-teeth letters of its group, and apart from gh (rafe gimal), which is the back-of-the-throat sound.
